annotations.annotation_text: The circular granite firing platform atop the Sandycove Martello Tower (Tower No. 11, built 1804 by the British Board of Ordnance). It served as an emplacement for a rotating 24-pounder cannon facing out across Dublin Bay. In 1904, Gogarty leased it from the War Office for £8 a year.
sources: Gifford, Don. Ulysses Annotated. UC Press, 1988, p. 13.
Joyce, James. Letters of James Joyce, Vol. II. Viking Press, 1966.

annotations.target_phrase: The snotgreen sea. The scrotumtightening sea.
annotations.annotation_text: Mulligan's notorious compound epithets. Parodies classical Homeric formulas ('wine-dark sea', epi oinopa ponton) through visceral bodily realism and mock-medical vernacular. Also alludes to the emerald green flag of Irish nationalism and the Greek sea god Proteus.
sources: Gilbert, Stuart. James Joyce's Ulysses. Faber, 1930.
Kenner, Hugh. Ulysses. Johns Hopkins University Press, 1987.

annotations.target_phrase: The rage of Caliban at not seeing his face in a glass
annotations.annotation_text: Direct quotation from Oscar Wilde's preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891): 'The nineteenth century dislike of Romanticism is the rage of Caliban not seeing his own face in a glass.' Caliban represents the savage, colonized subject in Shakespeare's The Tempest; here Mulligan casts Stephen as the resentful, melancholic poet gazing into the cracked lookingglass of Ireland.
sources: Wilde, Oscar. The Picture of Dorian Gray. Ward, Lock and Company, 1891.
Thornton, Weldon. Allusions in Ulysses. UNC Press, 1968, p. 14.

annotations.annotation_text: Stephen's stinging definition of Irish art under British and Vatican colonial subjugation. Synthesizes Wilde's aphorism with Swift's Preface to The Battle of the Books ('Satyr is a sort of Glass, wherein Beholders do generally discover every body's Face but their Own'). Establishes the domestic servant status of Ireland.
sources: Ellmann, Richard. James Joyce. Oxford UP, 1982, p. 131.
Gifford, Don. Ulysses Annotated. UC Press, 1988, p. 15.
